Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.)

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.)

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Where to eat in Barcelona, Spain, according to a local gastronomic tour guide

All-inclusive escapes have never looked — or tasted — so good

Today guests expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it

#6373. A Single Fluorescent Dye Can Now Reveal 14 Different Structures Inside Living Cells

Researchers at Peking University have developed a fluorescent dye that can distinguish at least 14 membrane-bound structures in living cells using subtle differences in their chemical environments

Watching the inner workings of living cells has long been difficult because most fluorescent dyes highlight only one cellular structure at a time. Now, researchers at Peking University have developed a dye called JONR that can distinguish at least 14 different structures using a single stain.

The dye changes color depending on the chemical environment surrounding it, allowing scientists to identify cellular structures without labeling each one separately. In laboratory tests, JONR identified organelles with three times the accuracy of Nile red, a fluorescent dye that has been used for more than a century.

JONR is based on Nile red, which glows differently depending on its surroundings. It produces greener light in oily environments and redder light in more polar ones. However, Nile red’s limited color changes make it difficult to tell similar cell membranes apart.

By modifying the dye’s molecular structure, the researchers increased its sensitivity to subtle differences between membranes. JONR also produces very little light in water, reducing unwanted background signals and making cellular structures easier to observe.

Using JONR, scientists were able to track interactions between structures inside living cells. They observed moving compartments called late endosomes pulling thin tubes of the endoplasmic reticulum, a network involved in processing proteins and other cellular activities.

The dye also revealed differences in how tightly molecules are packed within membranes. With specialized microscopy, researchers could examine both membrane composition and molecular organization using the same stain.

Experiments involving nerve cells showed that JONR could detect how molecules are arranged along nerve fibers. Additional tests in migrating cells revealed differences between the membranes of structures involved in cell movement.

The dye showed no significant toxicity in cultured cells, but the research has not yet demonstrated its performance in living animals or humans. Some measurements also require specialized microscopes.

Although further testing is needed, JONR could allow researchers to study several cellular structures and their interactions without relying on multiple fluorescent dyes.

Reference: “Far-red-emitting Nile red with boosted solvatochromism enables multidimensional imaging of membrane heterogeneity and dynamics” by Mingqiao Liu, Yunzhe Fu, Xiaopeng Li, Haolin Zhang, Yumiao Ma, Meiqi Li, Chunyan Shan, Hongxi Zheng, Xiaoyi Lu, Yan Zhang, Li Yu, Peng Xi and Zhixing Chen, 23 February 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101319

Funding: Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province (Major Basic Research Project), National Key Research and Development Program of China, Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission, Beijing National Laboratory for Molecular Sciences, National Natural Science Foundation of China

#6372. Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

The more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions. Though our current search for potentially habitable worlds is mostly restricted to finding rocky planets with liquid water and atmospheres, it will have to advance well beyond that to bear fruit. Things like exoplanet plate tectonics to keep climates moderate, and stars with long, stable lifetimes that let life fluorish and evolve are factors in habitability.

New research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains. The research is titled "Raising mountains for a habitable Earth," and it's published in Science Advances. The lead author is Dr. Matthijs Smit of the University of British Columbiaâs Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences.

Their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes important chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere. That, in turn, led to the eventual appearance of complex life.

"The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability," the authors write.

K2 is the second tallest mountain in the world. The crust underneath it is some of the thickest in the world. Research shows that in Earth's past, the crust thickened in some places, leading to the growth of very tall mountains. Increased weathering from those mountains preceded the planet's episodes of oxygenation, and researchers hypothesize that episodic spurts of mountain growth enabled Earth's habitability, and the eventual appearance of complex life. Image Credit: By Zacharie Grossen - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/42469860

"Continental silicate weathering controls the oceanward flux of carbon and bioactive nutrients that limit marine primary productivity, thus exerting control on atmospheric chemistry, climate, and marine biomass and biodiversity," they explain. "The majority of the global terrigenous runoff derives from mountainous regions."

The researchers focused on the last three billion years of Earth's history. They examined metamorphic rocks that were pushed deep underground by overlying tectonic plates. When mountains formed where plates collided, the mountains were able to reach much greater heights. That raised nutrient levels in the oceans, which helped photosynthesizing lifeforms oxygenate Earth's atmosphere.

âChanges that occurred deep in the Earth ultimately gave rise to much taller mountains over time, which may have made our planet habitable by providing the nutrients needed for life to form and flourish,â lead author Smit said. âNutrients such as phosphorous are essential ingredients for life on our planet, but prior to three billion years ago, these elements were locked in the Earthâs crust and the oceans were quite nutrient-starved. All this changed when tall mountains started to develop.â

The research shows that two periods of peak metamorphic pressure inside the planet, between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, led to thicker crusts in mountain-forming regions, and that let taller mountains form. The growth of Earth's mountains spiked, and those orogenic growth spurts were synchronous with other important changes on the planet.

âThe first growth spurt may have led to the emergence of land on a large scale for the first time, while the second growth spurt thrust mountain ranges to enormous heights,â said co-author Dr. Douwe van Hinsbergen of Utrecht University, The Netherlands. âGiven such profound effects, mountains may well have played a far greater role in the creation of a habitable planet than previously assumed.â

Earth's atmospheric oxygen rose in distinct periods, and the most well-known and consequential one was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) from about 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago. The researchers say that by the time the GOE occurred, Earth's mountains had grown substantially. They rose from near sea-level to about half the height of the modern-day Himalayas. Another distinct period of rising atmospheric oxygen was the Neoproterozoic Oxygen Event (NOE) from around 700 million to 500 million years ago. Mountain growth spiked at that time, too, according to the researchers. Various other atmospheric factors and oceanic factors related to habitability and complex life increased, too.

This figure shows time on the x-axis and more other information throughout. Blue shows how atmospheric O2 pressure rose compared to modern levels, especially during the GOE and the NOE. Purple shows the rise of sulfur isotope diversity, a measure of biological sulfur metabolism over time, and grey shows the percentage of oceanic strontium that comes from continental mountain erosion. Green shows the rise of organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. The snowflake symbols show Earth's main icehouse stages. Image Credit: Smit et al. Science Advances 13 Nov 2026 Vol 12, Issue 46

The timing of these spurts of mountain growth coincided with the growth of crustal thickness in mountain belts. In these belts, the thickness of the upper accreted crust grows as plates collide. The first episode increased thickness from 30km to 60 km, and the second episode saw an increase to almost 90 km. âWe suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,â Dr. Smit said. âAs a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.â

"Causes for environmental upheaval culminating in the GOE and NOE have been sought in various external forcing mechanisms, such as increased runoff resulting from supercontinent breakup, enhanced weathering of basaltic rocks at low latitude, and a dwindling CO2 (carbon dioxide) flux from arc volcanism," the authors write. While the researchers agree that these are valid hypotheses, they also point out that they're transient. That doesn't match the "irreversible nature of global oxygenation," and other changes. They're also not restricted to periods preceding the GOE and NOE.

The two episodes of crustal thickening and resulting spikes in mountain elevation and erosion are a better fit. "In contrast to all of these processes, the orogenic growth associated with tectonic revolutions R1 and R2 broadly coincide with the major periods of environmental upheaval in terms of their approximate timing, paucity, and irreversibility," the authors write.

The researchers couldn't measure the height of long-gone mountains, but they were able to determine the density and thickness of ancient crust. Since crustal thickness and density correlate with mountain height, they could calculate the height of ancient mountains.

Earth's tallest mountains today, Mount Everest, K2 and Kangchenjunga, are almost certainly some of the tallest ever produced. They approach nine km above sea level, and the crust under them is about 80 km thick. That's twice as thick as other continents. They illustrate how crustal thickness generates tall mountains, and emphasize the hypothesis that mountain growth helped enable Earth's habitability.

âItâs likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,â said co-author Dr. Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. âItâs exciting to think that mountain belts were once non-existent and that their development over the past three billion years may have driven the environmental and biological change that shaped our planet.â

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

Alex Keshavarzi is a senior research fellow in particle physics at University College London in the U.K., where he is probing how the behaviors of muons (the heavier cousins of electrons) could reveal unknown particles and forces. He worked with Live Science as part of the Association of British Science Writers media fellowships program, which provides a unique opportunity for practising scientists, clinicians and engineers to gain experience at media outlets.

#6370. The 6 Most Reliable Walkie-Talkies for When You Need Them Most

Stay connected wherever you go with these durable, two-way radios built for everything from backcountry trips to emergencies.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around. Serious adventure seekers know it’s best to prepare for their outdoor escapades—whether they’re heading deep into the wilderness or staying close to home. If not, you risk injury or worse. From a reliable fixed-blade knife to a solid pair of binoculars for scouting the trail ahead, there’s a whole slew of gear to keep you safe outdoors.

Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness. Yet this humble piece of equipment plays an important role in helping you communicate with colleagues, friends, and family when you’re on the go. They’re also a smart backup in an emergency and a way to monitor the weather in untamed landscapes and far-off places.

Today’s walkie-talkies haven’t changed all too much in look and feel from their early days. But they’re nothing like the cheap, toy versions we used as kids when exploring backyard “wilderness.” Modern features like NOAA weather alerts, VOX (hands-free operation), and app-connected features provide safeguards and peace of mind—especially in faraway places.

Our guide below covers what to keep in mind and how to choose a walkie-talkie for work, play, and emergencies—and offers a closer look at standout models worth your money.

Our evaluation process combined rigorous field testing across a wide variety of walkie-talkies in different environments with extensive research from trusted online sources. Meehan’s in-field testing for his best two-way radio picks ranged from trekking deep into the backcountry on hut trips to communicating seamlessly while mountain biking to traveling around a city.

Recognizing that walkie-talkies serve a wide audience, we also considered other scenarios where dependable communication is essential—on construction sites, inside expansive venues like convention centers, and across large retail operations.

With this breadth of uses in mind, we reviewed models spanning a range of functions and price points, carefully weighing usability, durability, range, features, and cost. For radios we couldn’t test directly, we reviewed trusted sources and compared specs. We also factored in real-world customer feedback, ensuring our final selections reflect not only expert insights but also everyday user experiences.

These Midland radios have proven reliable in the city and the mountains. The two-pack is a great value and includes advanced features like hands-free VOX and NOAA weather channel monitoring.

It's one of the most versatile walkie-talkies in terms of power options. As part of a two-pack, you get a charging cradle for each, but you can also charge the device with a micro-USB cable and, if you’re in the field for multiple days and run out of power, you can switch the battery pack out for a new one or use three AA batteries to power it—though it is hard to get the cover off.

The radios are compatible with multiple accessories, like a hand-held mic-speaker or an earpiece-mic combo. The latter makes hands-free use even easier, like in a restaurant or store setting.

But in the end, this relatively affordable set of walkies has an ideal feature set for most people.

It shouldn’t surprise that a company known for its smartphones, like the Razr+, would add smartphone-like features to its top-line walkie-talkies. That’s exactly what Motorola did with its 800-series Talkabout line.

It uses the Talkabout app for iOS and Android devices to enable features other walkie-talkies can’t, like letting you use the 800 series as a sort of smartphone modem when there’s no cell service.

The app also lets you send texts or share your location with others using an 800-series radio and the app. This feature is unavailable on most walkie-talkies, since they’re just two-way radios. It also supports smart pairing and connects to Bluetooth devices, like headphones or earbuds.

Most walkie-talkies on the market are waterproof, or at the very least water-resistant, since they’re meant for outdoor use. But you’ll find it harder to find a two-way radio that can actually float. That’s where Cobra's floating walkie-talkies stand out.

Built to IPX7 waterproof standards, this radio can survive full immersion underwater and is designed to float—ideal for situations like water sports, boating, paddling, skiing, and backcountry adventures. This walkie-talkie can handle dunkings and wet environments where communication is critical, and its orange rubber exterior makes it easy to spot in choppy surf or on snow-covered slopes.

Best for whitewater kayakers, stand-up paddle boarders, or even families enjoying a long weekend on the boat, it's a solid pick when you want to stay connected without worrying about waterlogging. You won’t have to worry about sinking or failing when wet. This durability is also ideal for backcountry skiers or climbers who deal with wet conditions daily.

Extra features like voice-activated transmission (aka hands-free talking) and the ability to replay missed radio calls also pack a punch. With its 37-mile range, NOAA weather alerts, and an impressive 2662 channel combinations, this Cobra radio is more than just waterproof—it’s an essential tool for adventurers heading into rugged, remote environments.

In the end, it’s hard to deny the Rocky Talkie Mountain Radio's capabilities compared to others made for outdoor adventure. It could easily have been our top pick, but since not everyone goes on multi-day backcountry trips, the Mountain Radio is likely overkill for most.

Founded in 2019, RockyTalkie is a newcomer to the scene, but it has nailed it with this 2-watt FRS radio with great range. Even in forested, mountainous areas, we could still easily communicate over miles. It also had one of the longest-lasting batteries, even in freezing weather.

The Mountain Radio sports a really simple interface with just five buttons, and it’s easy to lock onto a channel. The radio also has a great speaker and microphone for transmitting and receiving calls and a bright green LED display that disappears when the radio isn’t actively transmitting or receiving.

We also appreciate the radio's rugged, rubberized outer shell and its two removable attachment points. The device uses carabiners rather than belt clips like most other two-way radios. That makes it easy to attach to just about anything—a harness, a belt loop, a backpack strap, a PFD, and more. The secondary attachment point uses smaller carabiners and a coiled leash, making it even harder to drop or lose.

The only thing we found lacking in the radio is that it can’t scan and play NOAA weather alerts, which would be very helpful in a backcountry setting with no access to cell service.

The Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio showcases backcountry endurance at its finest. It’s beefed-up, replaceable battery lasts up to six full days on a single charge. That’s nearly a week of reliable communication without scrambling for a power bank or solar panel to plug into while off-grid—making it one of the longest-lasting walkie-talkies in its class.

This two-way radio also shines for its durability, with an IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also includes NOAA weather alerts, dual-frequency monitoring, and up to 5 watts of transmitting power for extended range. An important note: you need a GMRS license to operate this radio legally in the field.

While its design is compact, it’s heavier than many other walkie-talkies we tested. That said, for the peace of mind that comes with extended battery life and a durable design that tops our list for its rugged, waterproof build, you can’t go wrong with this radio.

Bottom line: the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt is our go-to choice for lasting power and rugged dependability.

While it’s technically not a walkie-talkie, the Garmin InReach Mini 2 deserves a spot in any serious communication roundup. For backcountry adventures where two-way communication is less frequent or a walkie-talkie just won’t cut it, this pocket-sized satellite device becomes a lifeline—especially when cell service and radio coverage fail.

The InReach Mini 2 uses the Iridium satellite network to deliver global coverage wherever you roam. You can send two-way text messages, share GPS location, and trigger SOS alerts from literally anywhere in the world. This piece of tech is best described as a satellite phone stripped down to the essentials: sending and receiving messages without overcomplicating communications.

It weighs a mere 3.5 ounces, and its compact design lets you clip the sat-phone to your pack or strap, or slide it into your pocket. You can also sync the InReach Mini 2 with Garmin’s Earthmate app for easier texting if you have your phone with you on your adventures.

Another big selling point of this piece of gear over walkie-talkies is its 14-day lifespan—long enough for extended off-grid trips. Unlike FRS or GMRS walkie-talkies, which are limited by terrain and line-of-sight requirements, this communication device promises to keep you in touch with family and friends wherever your adventures take you. Even more importantly, it keeps you connected in an emergency.

While a walkie-talkie is a simple, handheld, portable two-way radio, not all are the same. Some are designed for indoor use, while others are meant for outdoor use. Some suit adventurers and sportspeople, while others offer features best suited to first responders. And, of course, some are designed for kids. When selecting the right two-way radios for your needs, there are plenty of factors to consider.

Most walkie-talkies are Family Radio Service (FRS) units with 2 watts or less of broadcasting power. These need no license. Devices that have more than 2 watts of broadcasting power, up to 50 watts, are called General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) units.

GMRS devices require an FCC license. However, as the folks at Rocky Talkie explain on their site, it’s pretty easy to get one online in the U.S. It costs $35 and is good for 10 years, covering everyone in your immediate family. The higher the wattage, the more transmitting power and range the walkie-talkie has, which generally means it uses more power and has a larger antenna. You can see that difference pretty clearly between the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio and the brand’s smaller 2-watt Mountain Radio.

Both types of units can broadcast on a range of channels, and each channel has wattage restrictions. Channels 1 through 7 can broadcast at up to 5 watts. Channels 8 through 14 can only broadcast at up to 0.5 watts. Channels 15 through 22 can broadcast at up to 50 watts, making them ideal for communications up to 30 miles apart in good conditions.

Not all two-way radios are designed with the same level of user-friendliness and a simple interface. The interface plays a big role in how easy the device is to use, especially when in the field with limited bandwidth for fidgeting with buttons and screen controls. Some radios keep things simple with large knobs and backlit buttons that let you seamlessly switch channels or adjust volume with a quick twist or tap—even while wearing gloves. Others rely on small digital menus that can be challenging to navigate, especially while on the go.

And some advanced walkie-talkies even require setup, such as programming frequencies through a computer and cables. While this may give more control, it can intimidate newer two-way radio users.

When comparing radios, pay attention to details like clearly marked buttons, backlit displays for night use, and easy setup processes. Features like one-touch scanning or memory recall can be great options when you need quick, efficient communication. Ultimately, the best radio delivers reliable performance without sacrificing user experience—especially when it matters most in the field.

Most two-way radios use replaceable batteries, usually AA or AAA, rechargeable batteries, or sometimes can use either. Units with rechargeable batteries are often more expensive, but usually have good longevity for trail and backcountry use. Some units recharge in a cradle but ideally also have a port for charging via a DC or USB cable, allowing you to power up from a backup battery as needed. We’ve left units on overnight before and still had power in the morning, and some will go into a low-power mode when left on. The battery will last longer if you use the walkie less or use a lower wattage mode, but that will also reduce its transmitting and receiving range.

Obviously, you want your devices to last a long time, and walkie-talkies should endure for years and withstand knocks and drops. That's why most don’t have touchscreens or even glass screens. Most should be able to withstand minor spills or rain, but if you know you’ll be using them primarily in the water, like on a fishing boat or white-water rafting and kayaking, you’ll want a walkie-talkie that’s waterproof and carries an IP67 rating or higher. If you’re using walkies in the backcountry or on a job site, you’ll want two-way radios that are ruggedized—like the DeWalt 2-Watt Heavy-Duty Walkie-Talkie or Rocky Talkies—and can withstand drops better than some others.

Walkie-talkies offer a few options for remote operation. Some will allow VOX or hands-free operation and are activated by your voice. Others have wired microphones and speakers that are handheld or worn on a lapel or shoulder strap. Others have an earpiece and microphone. Some modern walkie-talkies can actually pair with Bluetooth earpieces, also allowing for hands-free communication. This is great when wearing a motorcycle helmet or when a wire could get in the way of whatever you’re doing.

Some models have additional channel monitoring or communication capabilities, like operating on two frequencies at the same time. These are handy features, but using them will drain the battery faster while they’re on.

Walkie-talkies designed for outdoor use, for example, can monitor NOAA weather channels, giving you some insight into the weather and the conditions you may face while camping, driving off-road, hiking, or hunting that you otherwise wouldn’t be able to access.

Still others can communicate and monitor two channels at the same time. That could allow you to communicate with multiple teams at once. For instance, in a rescue situation, you could communicate with your friends on one channel and the local sheriff’s office or the search-and-rescue team on another without switching channels every time.

While all walkie-talkie channels are open to all users, some are generally used by certain groups and/or in certain areas. You can talk with local organizations to find out which channels they use and broadcast on.

To help people connect with like minds, some are encouraging what they call community channels. These help people in a local backcountry area communicate with each other. Rocky Talkie lists some active community channels for local areas. While these channels help in some situations, you also don’t want to communicate constantly on channels monitored by SAR or local sheriff’s offices, because you could interrupt emergency operations.

Walkie-talkies come in a wide range of prices, and more expensive models often offer more benefits and features. So, while you can get a serviceable pair for about $30-$35, they won’t have much range or additional features. For a top-tier single walkie-talkie with multi-channel monitoring, high wattage and range, and water- and shock-proofing, you can expect to pay over $150 per unit.

Range is one of the biggest selling points for walkie-talkies, but it’s also one of the most misunderstood. Sure, the box may say “up to 35 miles of range.” That’s only if conditions are near-perfect—think one person on a mountain peak and another down in a valley, with nothing but clear air between them. In reality, terrain, obstructions, severe weather (like a snowstorm), and more can drastically cut that range. Dense forest, rocky canyons, massive hills, and buildings can shrink that range even more.

Most consumer FRS models perform best up to five miles, depending on the terrain. For most outdoor adventures, a reliable one-to-five-mile range is typical and usually enough to keep track of groups across rivers, campsites, or trails. GMRS radios, which we mentioned require a license, can stretch much further than five miles, especially when paired with repeaters.

Our recommendation: Shop for a walkie-talkie model and range based on realistic expectations for your use case, not the maximum range advertised in the brand’s marketing.

It depends! How often and for how long do you plan to use your radio? Are you looking for a basic radio or one built to perform off-grid? Battery life depends most on design and how often you use it. Most walkie-talkies advertise a battery lifespan of eight to 20 hours of runtime, but those numbers assume moderate to infrequent use. Continuous transmission drains the battery much faster than standby mode.

For shorter day hikes and quick outings, you won’t have to worry much about your radio lasting more than a single charge. On longer excursions, opt for a walkie-talkie that can be charged via USB-C with an external battery pack, or that uses AA or AAA batteries. Simply put: Don’t trust what the packaging says. Instead, consider how long you plan to use the two-way radio and whether you’ll have a chance to recharge partway through a long adventure.

Many modern two-way radios offer more than basic push-to-talk functionality. NOAA weather alerts are especially helpful for backcountry safety, providing real-time updates on weather patterns and severe storms heading your way.

Another feature to look for is VOX—voice-activated transmission—which enables hands-free use. Paddlers, bikers, and skiers are prime candidates for VOX-equipped walkie-talkies when devices aren’t always easy to grab while in motion.

For simple day-hiking trail use or communicating with your family across the campground, simple models will work just fine. But on bigger adventures like backpacking into the wilderness and remote paddling, investing in a two-way radio with all the bells and whistles gives you peace of mind and the right tools when conditions are worse than expected.

Erica Zazo (she/they) is a Chicago-based freelance writer covering outdoor news, gear, and guides for Backpacker Magazine, Outside, and more. She’s a big fan of urban nature, exploring lesser-known trails and towns, and the Midwest. Follow her adventures on Instagram: @onecurioustrvlr.

Chris Meehan is an internationally published writer, author, and editor with more than two decades of professional experience. He has authored multiple adventure guidebooks with Falcon Guides and his work focusses primarily on the nexus between sustainability and outdoor adventure. He is an experienced gear reviewer, tester, and travel writer who has explored multiple continents.
