#6258. The 7 Best Fireproof Home Safes Protect Your Valuables from Extreme Heat

Your standard safe may stop burglars, but can it also withstand fires and floods?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good home safe will protect your most important items from theft and damage, but if you want one that will also offer protection from heat, direct flames, and even water (in some cases), you need a fireproof home safe. This protection isn’t just limited to non-flammable items like jewelry or firearms, either. High-quality fireproof safes keep cash, important documents, photographs, and passports safe, too.

To go one step further, home safes rated as fireproof will protect your belongings from house fires and sprinkler systems, but if you're looking for protection from natural disasters, there are solutions out there. A safe rated for extreme temperatures will safeguard your things in the event of a wildfire, and those with airtight seals should prevent water from seeping in even during a flash flood.

We’ve reviewed the best fireproof home safes below with picks that cover your needs regardless of what you’re storing or how much space you need.

We made our choices on this list based on extensive research, looking closely at key features, brand reputation, and of course, each model’s temperature and fireproof rating. We also looked through customer reviews, making note of how well their safes held up in real-world situations. Beyond this, we took into account recommendations from professional firefighters. Because of these factors, you won’t see a wide variety of brands on this list.

In previous versions of this article, we featured fire safes and chests that were tested out by our team. While these models have since been discontinued or are out of stock, we used this experience to inform new choices for this list. All the safes on this list are “true” fireproof options, meaning that the safe itself will hold up, not just an included fireproof envelope. Each safe we selected is rated to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 degrees Fahrenheit.

More to Explore: Best Outdoor Security Cameras • Best Video Doorbell Cameras • Best Carbon Monoxide Detectors • Best Smart Locks

As you’ll see throughout this list, we believe in SentrySafe as a top brand for fireproof safes—for its lifetime warranty, $50,000 fire protection guarantee, and reliably high levels of fire protection across all products. This mid-sized, 1.23-cubic-foot option is the perfect choice for most people.

Alongside a fire rating of up to 1,700 degrees F for a full hour, the safe boasts a fully waterproof design that protects internal items completely for up to 24 hours in up to 8 inches of submerged water.

Beyond the powerful protection it offers, the fireproof safe also has internal organization features like key hooks, a shelf, and a lockable drawer for especially valuable items. The interior of the safe is even lit to help you see inside. That said, both the lights and the digital keypad are battery-operated, so you'll need to periodically replace them.

The safe, as a whole, weighs close to 90 pounds. While this is a great deterrent from a thief trying to simply steal the entire safe, it can make it quite difficult install or carry up stairs on your own.

As an affordable yet durable alternative to some of the higher-end models on our list, this safe from Amazon Basics checks a lot of our boxes. At 1.24 cubic feet, it's actually slightly larger than our Best Overall choice from SentrySafe, leaving you with just as much space inside, including a top shelf for organization.

The safe also comes with a digital keyboard for easy access. If the keyboard is damaged during a fire, the safe also comes with a backup emergency key that unlocks the mechanism manually.

The biggest detractor for this safe is its durability. The safe is only rated to handle up to 1,200 F for 20 minutes. This is considerably lower than many other safes on this list both in temperature and duration.

If you require more space and organization than our previous recommendations, this safe provides plenty. With over 2 cubic feet of space, there is significantly more room to store larger valuables, such as photo albums or antiques.

Furthermore, the internal organization boasts a top tray and a large bottom drawer, as well as key hooks and a small storage cubby on the door. Unlike other models on this list, the safe uses a dial lock which doesn't require batteries, but it can be cumbersome to use.

Like all SentrySafe models, this one will protect your items for up to an hour at 1,700 F and prevent moisture damage for 24 hours in 8 inches of water. This impressive durability extends to the outer strength of the safe, as well, which can handle a fall from 15 feet without significant damage. Because of its size and strength, the safe weighs a hefty 125 pounds.

Unlike the more traditional safes we recommend, this option from SentrySafe functions more like a secure file cabinet than a traditional safe. The chest holds up to 40 hanging files for easy document organization and has a small space on the lid for handheld items like passports or electronics.

While the safe gives up some fire protection compared to the classic options on our list (it’s rated for 30 minutes at 1,550 degrees), it more than makes up for this with its robust water protection. The file storage box can be fully submerged in water for up to 72 hours without the items inside seeing any water damage at all.

At 39 pounds, this safe is slightly more portable than the bulkier home options, though it is still relatively cumbersome to transport given the lack of handles or wheels.

This Sanctuary model stands out as the gold standard for fire protection. It’s capable of withstanding a blistering 1,800 F for 90 minutes. That makes it the best home safe to protect your valuables from the extreme heat of wildfires.

Additionally, with ETL-rated waterproofing, it can hold out for 7 days in up to 6 inches of standing water. The company also provides a lifetime warranty against fire, natural flood, and theft.

The LED-lit interior has two upholstered shelves and is California DOJ-certified for firearm storage. For security, the electronic lock has a timed lockout mode and tamper indicator. You can also enable an optional silent entry mode for added discretion.

Once you get this compact safe situated, at over 62 pounds, it’s not likely you’ll want to move it again. But, its sturdiness and heavy-duty construction are worth the extra money.

If you only need to protect a few small items, like your passport, a USB drive, and some jewelry, there’s no need to invest in such a large safe. This lock box safe from SentrySafe is small enough to be hidden away on a shelf in your closet, but it doesn’t sacrifice fire protection in the name of being compact.

Rated to handle up to 1,550 degrees F for up to 30 minutes, the lock box should be able to withstand house fires without much issue. The carrying handle also makes it easy to take this safe with you if you are evacuating the fire quickly.

Of course, because of its small size, there’s no internal organization. Everything just sits in the same compartment. But it’s not a feature-less safe. If you are interested in additional theft prevention, it comes with a bolt-down kit for securing the safe to your floor.

For security beyond just the physical integrity of the safe, the Mycube offers a biometric fingerprint scanner as the primary way to unlock its door. The safe saves up to 10 unique fingerprint IDs, so you can program it to open for you and your immediate family with ease.

If someone else needs access to the safe, you can also program a backup password they’ll enter from the digital keypad. Internally, the safe has a removable drawer for storing documents, small valuables, and watches. This also leaves the main compartment of the safe open for larger items.

The Mycube fire safe is quite durable with the company claiming it is capable of withstanding 1,700 F for up to an hour. Its worth noting that Mysafe does not use UL for its fire rating, though the company does report that the rating it has would be the equivalent of one from UL.

To withstand high temperatures, choose a safe that is completely fireproof rather than a security safe with a fire-resistant envelope. Unless all of your valuables fit comfortably in a fire-resistant envelope, the risk of damage to other items in the safe is far too high. Even in the envelope, your items will not be protected to the same degree as a completely fireproof safe.

For advanced protection, fireproof safes should withstand temperatures of at least 1,150 F for 30 minutes or more. In the case of wildfire risk, a fireproof safe that protects at temperatures up to 1,800 F is your best protection. Keep in mind, though, that wildfires get as hot as 2,000 degrees, which would melt most of the safes included here. Any safe you purchase should have fireproof ratings certified by either the Underwriter’s Laboratory (UL) or the inspection firm Intertek, designated by an “ETL” mark.

There are several different types of locking mechanisms available depending on the level of security you desire. Among our recommendations, you’ll find models with traditional keys, combination locks, and electronic keypads. Some safes also come with biometric locks that only unlock to your specific fingerprint, which may offer an additional layer of security.

The size of the valuables you need to store and the available space in your home will dictate the ideal dimensions for your fireproof safe. Look for a deeper safe if you need to protect a large cache of valuables or a variety of different-sized items.

Some smaller safes, like the Honeywell Small Safe Box Chest, are shaped like briefcases and work best for holding important documents. Similarly, if you are looking to store jewelry, look for deeper safes equipped with drawers or trays to better organize your items.

For a fireproof safe you can transport, look for a fireproof chest or document box that weighs 30 pounds or less. These safes are also light enough to be placed on a shelf. Heavier fireproof home security safes (upwards of 75 pounds and designed to deter thieves) usually specify and provide hardware for floor mounting.

Many fireproof safes that are water-resistant or waterproof may only be so under certain conditions, such as standing water of 5 to 8 inches, and possibly for only a certain duration of time. This ensures added protection of the safe’s contents when sprinklers go off in an apartment complex, or if the safe is in the direct line of heavy-duty hoses. Some fireproof security boxes or chests offer waterproof ratings anywhere from 8 to 72 hours spent submerged, which are optimal for homeowners who may face flood risks.

Fireproof rating is easily the most important feature to consider. An independent testing agency must rate the safe, and it should be able to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 F. However, we recommend much higher for those who are worried about wildfires.

Beware of home security safes that companies list as fireproof, but aren't rated by a testing agency. Many of these safes do not have fireproof bodies and instead just include a small fire-resistant envelope to store sensitive items in.

Once the temperature on the safe interior gets above 350 F, any paper inside (including all your hard-earned cash) is at risk of scorching. Even rooms in a burning house that aren’t on fire can get above 600 degrees F at eye level, which is definitely hot enough to soften steel.

There are many things you can and should keep in a fireproof safe, but if it you need to keep the items chilled or temperature controlled, it shouldn’t go in the safe long term. Avoid storing volatile chemicals or batteries in a safe as they can deteriorate or spill and damage other valuables.

You might assume most safes are lock it and forget it, but they do require some maintenance. You should “air out” your safe to avoid moisture build-up every few weeks to a few months depending on the climate where you live and the contents of your safe. You should also replace the batteries in battery-powered safe locks once a year.

Avoid installing a safe in the master bedroom, where security experts indicate thieves are most likely to check for valuables first. Fireproof safes are heavy, so it’s preferable to store them on the floor even though it might make it harder for you to access.

In fact, large standing safes often have mounting hardware included so you can bolt them into the floor of your basement or garage for additional security and stability.

#6257. Parasite outbreaks in the food supply chain highlight how much public attention hurts bagged salad sales

Google searches for "cyclospora" predicted where bagged salad sales fell during parasite outbreaks.

A food recall looks like a supply problem: bags pulled from the shelf, a gap in the produce case. During six cyclospora outbreaks between 2018 and 2022, stores showed no sign of cutting back on bagged salad, and prices barely moved, yet households bought less of it anyway.

Weekly purchases ran 3.89 percent below normal, on average, across those outbreak and recall periods, and the missing sales added up to roughly $374 million.

Where sales fell depended not only on where people got sick but on where people were typing “cyclospora” into Google.

Xuerui Yang ran the analysis as a doctoral student at The Ohio State University. She is now a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS).

The dollar figure is an estimate from household purchase records, and the search counts stand in for a region’s exposure to cyclospora outbreak news, not for what any one shopper read.

In an interview with Earth.com, Yang put the main lesson in one line. “News travels through media markets, not state lines,” she said.

Cyclospora cayetanensis, a single-celled parasite first identified in 1993, can live in soil or water for months. It survives the chlorine washes that processing plants run produce through.

Like other kinds of food poisoning, the infection usually brings watery diarrhea, cramps, bloating and a lost appetite, and most people recover on their own.

People with weakened immune systems can become severely ill or stay sick for a long time.

Large cyclospora outbreaks were rare before 2018. That year, reported outbreaks were tied to 1,165 illnesses nationwide, and the numbers have stayed high since. Packaged salads have been implicated more and more often.

Yang’s team picked six large multistate outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. Four of them traced to bagged salad mix. Together, they accounted for 2,157 illnesses, about two-thirds of every outbreak-linked case reported to the CDC in that span. The rest were smaller events.

Recalls followed the 2018, 2019 and 2020 outbreaks. The 2018 and 2020 salad recalls were traced to a single U.S. manufacturer and spread to store brands. The last two outbreaks in the study ended with no recall at all.

Earlier research on food scares measured public attention through news coverage, which is usually counted by state or for the whole country.

Yang’s team used something finer: how often people searched Google for “cyclospora,” week by week, in each of 210 media markets.

Nielsen draws those markets to map which TV and radio stations a household receives, and they follow broadcast signals rather than borders, so one market can straddle two states.

A second index, built from the public Google Trends tool, tracked general searches for salad, lettuce and basil, with outbreak terms filtered out.

The team matched both against weekly purchase records from a NielsenIQ panel of about 46,000 households a year, 12 million household-weeks in all.

The search index behaved the way a news measure should. Spikes in “cyclospora” searches lined up with spikes in news coverage.

During the 2020 cyclospora outbreak, search activity broadly followed where illnesses were being reported, and Illinois and Iowa reported the most.

Searches for “cyclospora” were linked to the steepest declines in purchases, and general searches about salad and leafy greens were linked to much smaller ones.

The authors read that as information working in two directions. News that names the parasite raises alarm, while ordinary searching about salad tends to settle it.

Recalls mattered on their own. A single week of a cyclospora recall cut purchases in affected states by about 3.2 percent compared with ordinary weeks, and recall periods ran 22 to 31 weeks.

Households whose salad purchases included one recalled brand bought no less than usual, but households whose purchases included two or more recalled brands bought noticeably less. One recalled brand, it seems, made little difference; a second one did.

“What people read online shows up in what they put in their carts,” Yang said.

To check that worry rather than empty shelves explained the decline, the team pulled store-level sales records for 2018 and 2020, the two years with salad recalls.

Store by store, across more than 100 million transactions, there was no sign that retailers cut what they stocked, and prices barely moved.

Media markets gave the team a natural test. In the authors’ example, someone in Washington, D.C., watches the same local news as someone in Virginia.

So a Virginia cyclospora outbreak reaches D.C. households even when no contaminated salad was ever sold there.

In states with no reported illness, households that shared a media market with an affected state bought 3.33 percent less salad per week than in outbreak-free weeks. Those households were a small slice of the data, so the estimate is less precise than the main one.

Yang doesn’t read that as a case for softer warnings. “People in unaffected states still bought less salad when they shared local news with an affected state,” she told Earth.com.

“And we don’t see this as a reason for quieter warnings. When shoppers stayed away from affected products, they’re also protecting themselves. What matters is clear, timely information.”

The 2020 outbreak was the biggest in the study, with 771 illnesses across 14 states. Counting the recall that followed, it reached 33 states and more than 190 million people, and it produced the largest loss, close to $190 million.

The bigger outbreak, though, drew the smaller reaction from shoppers.

Purchases fell about 3.1 percent in 2020 against 4.6 percent two years earlier. Furthermore, the 2020 estimate was weak enough that chance can’t be ruled out as the explanation. Searches for “cyclospora” were also lower and more scattered that year.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her about the smaller reaction, Yang pointed to timing. “Shoppers barely reacted until the recall came,” she said.

“Once specific products were named, purchases dropped. 2020 was also the summer of COVID, and that likely pulled attention away from other health news.”

The 2018 outbreaks cost about $79 million, roughly 1.6 percent of a bagged salad market worth about $4.91 billion a year by the industry estimate the authors cite.

Yang’s earlier work put the retail cost of each of two salmonella outbreaks tied to onions above $1 billion. The authors attribute part of that gap to salmonella being a name that more shoppers recognize.

Google searches catch people looking for information online and miss what they hear on TV, on the radio or from a neighbor. Regions that get their outbreak news offline may be underrepresented.

The search data also can’t show what any individual shopper read, so the results describe regions, not people.

The CDC records the date of a first illness, which comes before the public hears anything. So the study measured changes over whole outbreak-and-recall windows rather than the first days of alarm.

This year’s record, roughly 20,000 confirmed cyclospora cases by the CDC’s count, falls outside the study.

Yang said it raises the questions she would like to explore next: how the scale of the outbreak and the shifting information shaped what people bought.

For a shopper standing in the produce aisle in the middle of one, she had plainer advice. “Follow the official alerts,” she said. “Early on, the source information is often unclear, so if you can’t tell where your salad came from, it’s fine to avoid it for a while.”

“Once a product is confirmed, check whether your salad is on the recall list,” Yang said. “Washing won’t effectively remove the parasite.” Cooking, she added, kills it.

The full study was published in the journal Risk Analysis.

#6256. Tiny changes in your pupil size and blinking rate reveal how hard your brain is working

An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.

A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task shows up in the eyes. Pupils open wider and blinks come faster, and a VR headset with an eye tracker inside can record both.

A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard. The answer was mostly yes for healthy volunteers, and not yet for the patients.

Jordan Tsigarides of the University of East Anglia‘s School of Health Sciences led the study, which was part of his Ph.D., with colleagues at UEA and the University of Southampton.

Virtual reality is already used as a drug-free way to ease pain, he said. His goal is a headset that changes what it shows, based on how a patient is coping.

“Imagine putting on a VR headset that can recognize when you’re becoming mentally tired or overwhelmed and automatically adjust the experience to suit you,” Tsigarides said in an interview with Earth.com.

“On a difficult day, it might simplify an activity or guide you through a calming environment.”

The study tested only whether the headset could read the effort. It didn’t treat anyone’s pain.

Between March and June 2025, 84 adults put on a consumer VR headset with built-in eye tracking and played a memory game.

Half had lived with musculoskeletal pain for at least three months, most often rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis or fibromyalgia.

The other half were healthy university students and staff. They were younger on average, 35 years to the patients’ 58.

Letters appeared one at a time on a gray panel, each for three-quarters of a second. At the easiest level, a player pressed a button when a letter matched the one just before it. At the hardest, the match was four letters back. The whole session lasted under 20 minutes.

Players found it hard, and said so. Their own ratings of effort kept climbing through the top level, even after their scores had stopped getting worse.

Pupils widened as the levels got harder, by about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) at most, which is less than the thickness of a credit card. Blinks came more often too.

Both changes showed up in people with chronic pain and in people without it, and pain and fatigue scores made no difference to either one.

“What fascinated me was that people’s eyes responded to mental effort in remarkably similar ways, whether or not they lived with chronic pain,” Tsigarides told Earth.com.

A plain average of pupil size told a computer almost nothing. A simple model that used average pupil size alone to sort the easiest level from the hardest guessed right 56 percent of the time in healthy volunteers.

In patients it managed 51 percent, which is barely better than chance. The pattern was in the way the pupil changed second by second, not in its size.

Machine learning models that read the full, second-by-second trace did much better, at least in healthy volunteers. Tested on people they had never seen, the best models picked the easy level from the hard one with 88 percent accuracy.

In the chronic pain group, the same models managed 58 to 65 percent.

Age didn’t explain the gap. When the team matched volunteers and patients by age, or adjusted for it, the patients’ eyes were still harder to read.

The two groups also differed in education, medication and other illnesses, and the authors said a sample of 84 can’t untangle all of that.

The patients were a varied group. Nearly all had two or more long-term conditions, and 45 percent took opioids. A quarter had dry eyes or another eye problem. None of those factors, on its own, predicted whose eyes the models misread.

“Rather than expecting one algorithm to work for everyone, we may need headsets that learn how each individual responds,” he said.

One result was encouraging. People with chronic pain rated their motivation above 90 out of 100 at every level of the game, the same as the healthy group. Motion sickness scores were low in both groups, and pain scores didn’t rise during the session.

Tsigarides holds an honorary chief medical officer role at Revolve Labs Ltd, a company that helped fund his Ph.D. The paper discloses both.

Virtual reality for pain has so far been a fixed experience, Tsigarides said: everyone gets the same woodland walk or the same puzzle, however they feel that day.

His earlier work tested VR therapy in people with fibromyalgia, and he said this study is a step toward a version that adjusts itself.

Everyone was measured once, on one day. The researchers can’t say whether a patient’s eyes behave the same way on a good day and a bad one, and Tsigarides says investigating that question comes next.

“Someone’s ability to concentrate might be very different on a good day compared with a day when their pain or fatigue is particularly severe,” he said.

The team also wants to move from a letter-matching game to the kind of calming scenes a real therapy uses, where changing light levels will complicate the pupil readings.

All of the models in this study were run afterward on a desktop computer rather than live inside the headset. None was tested on an outside group of patients.

Tsigarides told Earth.com he hopes early adaptive systems can be tested within a few years. Whether a headset that reads mental effort and responds to it actually eases anyone’s pain is a trial that hasn’t been run.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

Archaeologists found hundreds of bison bones at the Nighthawk bison jump site in Texas.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

Archaeologists excavating a bison jump site called Nighthawk in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6253. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”
